                          GAINER FAMILY’S INITIAL BRIEF

       COME NOW, Franklin and Jane Gainer, Sally Guitar, and Matthew and Mindy

Gainer (collectively, the “Gainer Family”) and file this Initial Brief in the above-captioned

proceeding in accordance with 16 Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”) § 22.124. The Gainer

Family respectfully show as follows:

       The Gainer Family filed its Statement of Position as Interchange Filing No. 3894 opposing

the N4 link included in the Application, which would traverse the Gainer Family’s property located

in Menard County, Texas. The Gainer Family continues to assert that the Commission’s criteria

and factors to be considered under state law for determining the route of a transmission line dictate

that the N4 link not be included in an approved transmission line route for the Project.




                                                     1
          The Gainer Family own property that would be traversed by proposed routes in the

Application, in particular alternative routes containing Link N4. 1 Franklin and Jane Gainer, and

Matthew and Mindy Gainer own property described by the Applicants as Tract Nos. 451-458.

Sally Guitar owns property described by the Applicants as Tract Nos. 448-450.

Characteristics of Property on the N4 Link

         The record includes descriptions of the characteristics of property on the N4 link—an

undisturbed terrain and viewshed; gravel roads away from the sounds of traffic and surrounded by

large neighbors; no windmills, power lines, cell towers, or views of roads. 2 The people in this area

operate profitable family-owned businesses run with passion and purpose.3 The Gainer Ranch

exemplifies these characteristics. Like the Stephens’s, the Gainer Ranch hosts regular, seasonal

recreational opportunities for hunters that would be severely impacted by the presence of a

transmission line across the Gainer Ranch.4 The Gainer Ranch’s cattle operations, its conservation

efforts, and its status as a heritage ranch would also be severely impacted.

Support for Route 894

         Based on the evidence in the record, the Gainer Family supports the Applicants’ conclusion

that Route 894 constitutes the “best meets” route. Route 894 is not a route advanced by intervenors

against the weight of the record. It is the route the Applicants themselves, after evaluating 1,246

alternative configurations and filing 122 of them for the Commission’s consideration, identified

as best meeting the statutory and regulatory routing factors.5

engineering information, and personal reconnaissance of the study area.6 LCRA TSC witness

Kelly Wells confirmed that LCRA TSC likewise supports Route 894 as the route that best

addresses the requirements of PURA and the Commission’s Substantive Rules. 7

estimated transmission line cost of $1,680,919,000 is only 2.73% above the least expensive filed

highest.10 It crosses no parks or recreational areas and has none within 1,000 feet of its

length.12 Across the routing factors the Commission must weigh, Route 894 consistently performs

at or near the most favorable end of the range, without the trade-offs that accompany the routes

intervenors have proposed in its place.

        Ryan Hopkins’ analysis also confirmed that Route 894 was the “best meets” route. 34 Mr.

Hopkins noted that Route 894’s “best meets” designation is not the product of a single dominant

metric. Rather, Route 894 is a consistently strong performance across the highest-weighted criteria

categories, broadly excellent across the categories. Route 894 was particularly strong in the

consideration of factors related to habitable structures (a consideration in the prudent avoidance

factor); total project cost; parks; cultural resources; aviation safety; and stream crossings.

        The Gainer Family respectfully requests that the Administrative Law Judges propose and

the Commission adopt Route 894 as the “best meets” route for this proceeding.

Opposition to Routes CCG, 572, and 296

opposition to Route 894 focuses on issues like impacts to recreational enjoyment, wildlife, and

hunting land; impacts to cattle grazing and livestock operations; aesthetic and visual impacts;

historical and cultural resources impacts related to Native American artifacts; among similar

issues. Each of these criticisms concern constraints or community values that would be present at

some point along every alternative route.”35

CCG has 105 habitable structures and ranks in Quartile 2. This constitutes a 20-structure

Route CCG has approximately 41 more structure-type identifications than Route 894.

This difference is again significant and material. Ms. Reinecke’s own Table RLSR-13 documents

that the top public priority in both Question 5 (land use) and Question 7 (community resources)

was minimizing impact on residential areas. 39 Route CCG, with 41 more structure-type

           In reviewing G6 and N4-specific issues, Ms. Reinecke’s analysis is also lacking. Ms.

Reinecke did not produce a Features Map for G2-G6; did not count habitable structures along G2-

support for the G2-G6 segment being included in a “best meets” route.

           The N4 substitution is completely unsupported and unjustified. Ms. Reinecke includes in

her testimony no written justification, no supporting exhibit, no field count, and no viewshed

analysis regarding the insertion of the N4 link. She provides no Features Map; no habitable

structures count; no analysis of ROW parallelism; no slope or stream-crossing inventory; or any

FAA airfield-clearance review for the N4 link. Without any analysis or justification, the record

does not support inclusion of the N4 link in a “best meets” route.

           Selection of Route CCG as the “best meets” route is not supported by the record.

his direct testimony, “The Link N12 and N4 would be a better fit.” He then proceeds to discuss the

attributes of the N12 Link. 49 Mr. Brewer provides no analysis of the N4 Link, other

than presumably it is a link that does not affect his client. Instead, he advocates specifically for the
